headline: A Woman's Backyard Camera Keeps Catching Coyotes at Her Water Bowl. One of Them Is Not a Coyote
dek: The pack comes back again and again, and the big dark stranger trots in with them every time. Nobody can work out where he came from.
body: Patricia Suflita Wilson keeps wildlife cameras running in her yard on the west side of Tucson, Arizona, and coyotes coming in for a drink at her water bowl are nothing new. What made her look twice was the animal walking along with them.

It was a dog. A big one, around 60 pounds, which Wilson thinks may be part boxer or part pit bull. It was not hiding, cornered or being chased. It was simply drinking with the pack, as if it belonged there.

Over the following two weeks the coyotes returned several times, and each time the dog was right there with them. Wilson gave him a name, Sombra, Spanish for shadow, and says everything about the way he behaves suggests the pack has taken him in.

Her first guess was that Sombra was Raven, a dog that had slipped away from Pima Animal Care Center earlier in the fall. The shelter studied her footage and concluded otherwise: the markings on the two dogs don't match. So Sombra's real story, and whether anyone is missing him, is still unknown.

body.quote: "For this dog, finding a way to trap it and not the coyotes could be very difficult," shelter spokesperson Nikki Reck told AZPM.

body: For now the shelter says it will only step in if Sombra looks like he is in danger or becomes a risk to people. Wilson, meanwhile, is hunting for a qualified trapper in case his health slips or he falls out with his new family.

Dogs being welcomed into coyote packs is rare, but it has happened before. In Nevada, a dog called Ghost lived with a group of coyotes for several months before people finally managed to bring him in.

headline: A Camera Set Up to Watch Minks in an Estonian Forest Films Something Else Entirely. Its Owners Call It a Unicorn
dek: The animal in the clip has one thing sticking straight out of the middle of its forehead. Experts still can't agree on what it is.
body: On Saaremaa, Estonia's biggest island, the Lutreola Foundation keeps trail cameras in the woods for one reason: to keep an eye on minks. The foundation works to bring back the European mink, one of the rarest mammals on the continent.
Trail cameras film whatever walks past, though, and recently one of them recorded a visitor the team had never seen before.

It was a roe deer, a common sight in Estonian forests. What was not common was its head. Instead of a pair of antlers on top, it had a single growth poking out from the middle of its forehead, pointing forward like something from a fairy tale.
The foundation shared the clip on Facebook and did not hold back, announcing that a unicorn had been found on Saaremaa and joking that little girls' dreams had finally come true.

The Estonian weekly Maaleht asked experts what they were looking at. From the footage alone, they couldn't say for sure. It might be a misplaced antler. It might even be an extra ear growing out of the centre of the deer's forehead.
Deer antlers normally sprout from two bony bases on the top of the skull, which is why a lone growth in the middle of the face looks so strange.
The unicorn was not the only surprise on the memory card. The same camera also caught a black stork, a shy forest bird that is far harder to spot than its white cousin.

headline: Hundreds of Rocky Balboas Storm the Philadelphia Museum Steps. Not All of Them Were Counted
dek: Grey sweats, black beanie, black high-tops. Guinness had a strict dress code, and a judge was checking.
body: Fifty years after Rocky first ran up the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the city threw a month of parties for its favourite fictional boxer. One of them was a world record attempt: the largest gathering of people dressed as Rocky Balboa.
On Friday, November 13, in cold drizzle, fans in identical outfits packed the famous steps. Guinness World Records needed at least 250 of them for the record to count.

There were rules. To be counted you had to wear a grey hooded sweatshirt and grey sweatpants, a black beanie and black Converse high-tops, the look Sylvester Stallone wore in his training montage. Some people got free costumes from the organisers. Others put theirs together from Amazon and Walmart.

A Guinness adjudicator walked the crowd before giving a number, and a handful of would-be Rockys were taken off the total because their outfits did not meet the rules. Even so, the final figure was well over double the minimum.

body.quote: "Philadelphia, today you achieved 570," adjudicator Andy Glass told the crowd, according to Billy Penn.

body: Once the record was official, the 570 Rockys did the only thing that made sense. They ran up the steps together and posed around the Rocky statue for a group photo.

Fans came from all over. A former wrestler from Allentown wrapped his hands in athletic tape from his school days. A couple flew in from Florida after failing to get an online registration and simply bought the pieces themselves. Several people said the same thing: everyone loves an underdog.

The weather did win one round. Cold and rain forced the city to postpone a rededication of the statue and cancel a Philly Pops concert. The record attempt went ahead anyway, which is very on-brand for Rocky.

headline: In 1960, Scientists Worked Out the Exact Day Humanity Would End: Friday, November 13, 2026
dek: The paper ran in one of the world's top science journals, and for decades its numbers were scarily accurate. Then something changed.
body: In November 1960 the journal Science printed a paper with one of the most alarming titles in its history: "Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026". It was written by the physicist Heinz von Foerster and two of his students, Patricia Mora and Lawrence Amiot.

Their argument was about people, not bombs or asteroids. The trio gathered 24 estimates of the world's population stretching back roughly 2,000 years and noticed that the time it took for humanity to double in number kept getting shorter.

Most living things grow, at best, exponentially. Humans, the authors argued, were different: because we talk, trade and team up, more people meant more cooperation, and more cooperation meant even faster growth. Run that curve forward and the doubling time hits zero. The population heads for infinity. They even put a date on it.

body.quote: "Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve. They will be squeezed to death." — von Foerster, Mora and Amiot, Science, 1960

body: Demographers and mathematicians lined up to write in and call the work ridiculous. The authors defended their math. The idea spread anyway, into textbooks, newspapers, a Canadian parliamentary committee and even a comic strip. The paper also cracked a dark joke about shipping surplus people into space with no return ticket.

body.h2: The awkward part: it kept working

body: For years the real numbers stayed embarrassingly close to the doomsday curve, closer than many professional forecasts in the 1970s and 1980s. Only around 1993, roughly halfway to the big day, did the world's actual population start falling behind.

The reason is the twist. The paper's own suggested escape route was to cut the global birth rate in half. Today the birth rate is a little under half of what it was in 1960. In other words, humanity more or less followed the prescription.

There were clues that von Foerster was not entirely serious. Before science he had worked as a magician, and 13 November happened to be his birthday. Researchers today see the paper less as a prophecy than as a clever way to point at a startling pattern. The date itself finally arrived on Friday, November 13 with rumours swirling on social media. In Vienna, a science centre marked it with a conference on the sense and nonsense of end-of-the-world predictions. The world, for the record, is still here.

headline: A Giant Golden Leg Pulled From a Scottish Bog Puzzled Experts for 200 Years. Now They Know Whose It Was
dek: Everyone assumed it was loot dragged north by raiders. The clean edge at the top of the boot told a very different story.
body: In 1820, someone digging in a bog at Milsington, near Hawick in the Scottish Borders, pulled out something that did not belong there: a bronze lower leg, bigger than a real one, finished in gold and ending in a carefully modelled boot.

Nothing like it has ever turned up in Scotland before or since. It is the only piece of a giant statue of a Roman emperor ever found north of the border, and for two centuries nobody could explain what it was doing in a peat bog.
The accepted answer was plunder. Experts assumed the leg had been hacked off a statue in a Roman city further south, perhaps York, and carried north as a trophy by local warriors.

Researchers at National Museums Scotland have now taken a fresh look and come to a very different conclusion. They believe the leg belonged to a towering gilded statue of the emperor Antoninus Pius riding a horse, similar to the famous bronze of Marcus Aurelius that still stands in Rome.

Antoninus Pius is the emperor who pushed Rome's frontier into Scotland and built the Antonine Wall. The team thinks his statue stood somewhere in the Borders in the AD 140s to celebrate the conquest of southern Scotland. A patch of missing gold around the knee suggests a cloak or tunic once hung over it.
The real surprise is at the top of the leg. There are no hack marks at all. The bronze ends exactly as it was cast, which means the statue was taken apart at its joints, not smashed.

That points the finger at the Romans themselves. When the army pulled back from southern Scotland in the 160s or 180s, it seems to have dismantled its own monument rather than leave the emperor behind. Roman troops did the same with altars and inscriptions along the Antonine Wall, burying them instead of abandoning them. Why one gilded leg ended up in a bog remains a mystery, and so does the spot where the statue stood.
A full-size reconstruction of the horse and rider is now on show at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh, in an exhibition about Roman Scotland that runs until April 2027.

headline: A Philosopher's Real Head Has Been Locked in a University Safe for Almost 200 Years. Scientists Just Scanned It
dek: His skeleton sits in a glass case, dressed in his own clothes. The head on top is wax. The real one finally got a check-up, and it explained a lot.
body: Jeremy Bentham, the English thinker behind utilitarianism, had unusual plans for his body. His will asked for it to be dissected in public for science and then preserved and displayed. He even coined a word for the result: an auto-icon, or self-image.

After he died in June 1832, his friend Thomas Southwood Smith did as asked. Bentham's skeleton was padded out, dressed in his own clothes and seated in a wooden cabinet. It can still be visited at University College London today.

The head was the problem. Smith tried to preserve the real one, but the result was so grim that he ordered a wax head to sit on the body instead. The genuine article now lives in a secure conservation safe.

To mark UCL's 200th anniversary, a team from the university's collections, its Hawkes Institute and its medical physics department ran the fragile head through a CT scanner. It was too big to fit the machine's field of view in one go, so they imaged the front and back separately and stitched the two halves together, without ever handling it.

The scans showed teeth in a dreadful state and a badly damaged lower jaw, with signs of arthritis. In other words, one of history's great thinkers about pleasure and pain spent years with crippling toothache.

body.quote: In an 1830 letter, Bentham wrote that he had more than once "submitted to the momentary torment to rid myself of the enduring one."

body: The scan also revealed a hole in the top of the skull where a metal rod once fixed the head to the body, a few traces of the tissue around the brain, which was removed during preservation, and a pair of beautifully crafted glass eyes, complete with anatomically correct optic nerves.

The team has printed a 3D copy of the skull and hopes to share the data so teachers can print their own. A Bentham expert at UCL said the man who donated his body to science would almost certainly have approved.

headline: A City Council Election Ends 711 to 711. The Winner Is Decided by a 52-Year-Old Coin
dek: Minnesota law says a tie must be settled "by lot." Both candidates were allowed to inspect the coin first. Only one got to call it.
body: Pine Island, a small city about 20 minutes north of Rochester, Minnesota, had two city council seats on the ballot on November 3. The first was settled the normal way. The second refused to be.
When every vote was counted, incumbent Delana Weis and challenger Dominick Pahl had exactly the same total: 711 votes each.

Minnesota has a rule for that. When an election ends in a tie, state law tells the local canvassing board to decide the result by lot, which in plain English means a game of chance. Pine Island went for the classic option.

On Thursday evening the city held a special meeting at City Hall. Both candidates were allowed to inspect the coin before it went into the air, to make sure there was nothing funny about it. As the incumbent, Weis got to call it.
She chose heads. The coin, a quarter minted in 1974, landed heads up. Weis keeps her seat.
Pahl took it well. He congratulated his rival, said he was glad Weis would be doing the job and told reporters he plans to run again.

There is a strange legal wrinkle. Under Minnesota rules, a recount can only happen after the losing side asks for one, which means the coin had to pick a winner first. Pahl could still request one, but by his own account he is happy to let the quarter have the final word.

headline: An Ohio Town Spends 45 Days Failing to Catch One Runaway Sheep. Then a Teenager Rides In on Horseback
dek: There was a Facebook event, a police department, an animal sanctuary and a lot of volunteers. None of it worked until the rope came out.
body: In September, people in Wadsworth, Ohio, started reporting a sheep wandering around town. Nobody knew whose it was, and nobody could get near it.
She was an American blackbelly, a hardy, athletic breed that turned out to be very good at not being caught. Over the following weeks she turned up in yards and fields, then vanished again.

The hunt grew into a town project. Janine Smalley, who runs Whispering Acres Farm Animal Sanctuary, and volunteer Rebecca Roxberry led the effort, a Facebook event called Catching the Wadsworth Sheep gathered sightings, and the Wadsworth Police Department joined in posting updates.

She was finally spotted in a field off U.S. Route 224, near a KFC, and guided back to the spot where Roxberry had been leaving food for her. That is where teenager Reagan Crumpler arrived on her 18-year-old horse, Catalena, with a rope.
Even then it was not quick. Crumpler said it took hours of chasing and several near misses before her lasso finally landed. Roxberry announced the capture that afternoon, ending a 45-day saga.

body.quote: "All that mattered is that we caught her, she's safe and sound, and she's in the best of care," Roxberry told News 5 Cleveland.

body: The sheep's new name includes Reagan, in honour of the girl who caught her. She is a little thin after six weeks on the run, so she is on a refeeding plan and due a vet check at the sanctuary.
Her owner has still not come forward. If nobody does, the escape artist has a permanent home at Whispering Acres.

headline: A €145,000 Golden Sculpture Vanishes From a Busy Art Fair in 15 Minutes. Police Say It Wasn't About the Gold
dek: Now the gallery is asking everyone who walked past for an unusual favour.
body: Art Cologne, one of Germany's oldest and biggest art fairs, was winding down on Sunday, November 8. At booth C-121, run by Düsseldorf's Galerie Ludorff, a small gold-coloured sculpture stood on its pedestal.
Somewhere between 4:55 and 5:10 p.m., it stopped standing there. Someone took it, and the pedestal was left bare.

The piece is S'élevant, or Rising, a 1962 gilded bronze by Hans Arp, the Franco-German artist known for smooth, curving, organic shapes. It is only 28 centimetres tall, about the height of a wine bottle, which presumably helped. Reports value it at between €135,000 and €145,000.
Cologne police were quick to rule out one motive. The metal itself is worth very little, a spokesperson said, so whoever took it was not planning to melt it down.

That points to the art market, and the gallery is betting the sculpture's distinctive rising curves will give it away if it is ever offered for sale. Dealers and collectors have been asked to keep watch.

It has also made an unusual appeal. Anyone who was near booth C-121 during those 15 minutes and took photos or videos is asked to send them in, in case something in the background shows who walked off with it.
The gallery called the theft a regrettable shadow over an otherwise very successful fair, and says it hopes the sculpture turns up unharmed.

headline: Two Unusual Passengers Climb Aboard a Detroit City Bus. Their Handler Says It's Not Their First Time
dek: The video went viral, the city launched an investigation, and the man behind it had a list of bus routes they had already tried.
body: Just after 5 p.m. on November 7, a Detroit Department of Transportation bus pulled up at a stop near 7 Mile and Strasburg Street. The doors opened and two horses walked on.
Two men led them on board and then back off through the rear door. A woman named Ellessia Drew filmed the whole thing and posted it to Facebook, and it spread fast.

One of the men was Jordan Williams, a co-founder of Urban City Cowboys, a group that teaches Detroit kids about horses and offers riding lessons and equestrian therapy for children with disabilities. He said he was heading home from a fundraiser and asked the driver if he could walk the horses through for a quick video.

He also said it wasn't a one-off. By his account, his horses had already been on buses on the Jefferson, Chalmers, Conners and 7 Mile routes. He joked that buses have got a lot smaller than they used to be, or that maybe he has got bigger.

The city was less amused. DDOT said the stunt went against its policy and could make for an unsafe and uncomfortable ride for passengers, and later released footage from the bus's own cameras. Officials said they had spoken to the driver.

body.quote: "I didn't mean to get anybody in trouble," Williams said, according to LiveNOW from FOX.

body: There is one small loophole. DDOT does allow service animals, and under federal rules a miniature horse can count as one. The city said these two were clearly on board for other reasons. Williams' hope is that officials take it as a joke and come out to a rodeo.

headline: San Francisco Crowns Its Best Elizabeth Holmes Look-Alike. The Winner's Day Job Is a Little Too Perfect
dek: Black turtlenecks, fake $100 bills and homemade blood-testing machines filled the park. The judges' pick turned out to have a medical gadget of her own.
body: On Saturday, November 7, San Francisco's Lafayette Park filled up with black turtlenecks. Around two dozen people had come to compete for the title of best Elizabeth Holmes look-alike, watched by a crowd of a few hundred.

Holmes is the Theranos founder who claimed her company could run a whole range of medical tests from a drop of blood, and who went to prison for fraud when it turned out it could not. The contest was inspired by You Can See Everything, a new documentary about her co-directed by Nathan Fielder, so there was a Fielder look-alike contest too.

Three roommates organised the event on Instagram, and their online invitation got 1,000 RSVPs almost as soon as it went live. 'Our whole mission is just to make SF fun again,' one of them, Tanvi Kaur, told the Stanford Daily.

Contestants brought red lipstick, stacks of fake $100 bills, homemade copies of Theranos's infamous Edison testing machine, and boxes of Tylenol and Mike and Ike sweets. The event was even sponsored by a Texas jerky brand that makes a cameo in the film.
Then the judges picked their winner: Sierra Stingl, a 30-year-old plastic surgery resident at Stanford, the university Holmes famously dropped out of to start her company.

body.quote: Stingl has also invented a medical device, a wearable monitor that uses light to check tissue after reconstructive surgery. "It's a little eerie, given my background," she told SFist.

body: The parallels stop there, though. Her device was convincing enough to inspire a storyline on Grey's Anatomy, where she made a guest appearance. She told the Stanford Daily she does not love the comparison, because integrity matters to her. She went home with a crown, a sash and a pair of headphones.

headline: Farmer Fixing His Fence Spots a Fence Post Lying in the Grass. He Doesn't Remember Dropping It
dek: It was about seven feet long and in roughly the right place. Then he took a closer look.
body: In early October, the animal shelter in Hoke County, North Carolina, put out a warning: a pet boa constrictor, six to seven feet long, had escaped from a home in the Calloway Road area near Raeford. Residents were told to keep their distance and call animal control if they saw it.
Weeks went by with no sign of it. Richard Wood, who farms four doors down from where the snake got out, admits he had more or less forgotten about it.

Then one Wednesday he was out repairing a fence with his daughter, Peyton, and noticed what looked like a fence post on the ground. He assumed one of the workers had dropped it. It turned out to be the missing boa, almost a month after it vanished.

Animal control said it would take about half an hour to get there, and Wood was worried the snake would slip off again in the meantime. So he called a friend who keeps large snakes and asked what to do. Picking it up himself, he decided, was not an option.

body.quote: "Peyton got it by the tail. I got it around by his head. He went right in," Wood told WNCN.

body: "In" meant a Rubbermaid storage tub. Officers arrived with Matthew George, known online as Mountain Matt, who took the snake into his care.

It turns out the owner had moved to Wilmington and left the boa with his father, and it escaped after its enclosure was moved into an outdoor building. Wood, for his part, thinks the snake was glad the adventure was over. It is staying with Mountain Matt until its owner collects it.

headline: Police Rush to a Break-In in Progress. They Find the Intruder Tucked Up in Bed
dek: She took an unusual route into the house. Then she seems to have decided to stay a while.
body: Just after 8 a.m. on a weekday morning in early November, officers from the Windsor Police Service's Amherstburg detachment were sent to a reported break-in in progress on Victoria Street South.
Amherstburg is a quiet, historic town where the Detroit River meets Lake Erie, about 25 miles south of Windsor. A burglary happening right now is not an everyday call there.
Officers believe the intruder got in by taking the cover off an air conditioning unit and climbing through the gap.
Once inside, she does not seem to have gone hunting for valuables. When police went through the house, they found her in one of the beds, fast asleep.
She was arrested without any trouble. The 46-year-old woman was charged with being unlawfully in a dwelling and with mischief under $5,000, and police said she also had an outstanding warrant.
Police did not say how long she had been sleeping by the time they arrived, or whether anyone was home when she climbed in.
The story quickly travelled far beyond Ontario, with TV stations across the United States picking it up.

headline: Two College Players Score Into Their Own Basket on the Same Night. One of Their Teams Still Wins
dek: Two different games, two wide-open layups, both at the wrong end, about an hour apart. Only one of the two had a happy ending.
body: Every basketball player has had the nightmare. You grab the ball, you see an empty hoop, you lay it in, and then the crowd makes a strange noise. On Friday, November 6, it happened for real in two US women's college games, about an hour apart.

The first came early in Northwestern State's game at Arkansas. Under pressure from the Razorbacks' full-court press, junior guard Karma Wynn took a bounce pass from a teammate right under her own basket. Nobody was guarding her. She calmly laid it in. It was the wrong hoop, and it put her side six points behind.
Under the rules a basket scored at the wrong end does not go to the shooter. It counts for the other team, so Arkansas collected two free points. Northwestern State never recovered and lost 89-59.

The second mistake came at a much worse moment. In Las Cruces, New Mexico State trailed Southern Utah by one with about 20 seconds left. Senior guard Emma Christiano read an inbounds pass perfectly, stole it, and raced in for an uncontested layup.

Again, wrong basket. The home broadcast did not notice at first either. Its play-by-play voice shouted that the Aggies had the lead, until the analyst pointed out that Southern Utah was now three points up.

body.quote: "Aggies lead!" the play-by-play announcer shouted, according to the AP. They did not.

body: Here is where the night took a turn. Freshman forward Stacy Chovino scored the Aggies' last two baskets, the second one at the correct end with about two seconds left. New Mexico State won 64-63, its first win of the season.
So two players made the same mistake on the same night. One team lost by 30. The other won by a single point and could laugh about it.

headline: Man Runs a Mile in Just Over Five Minutes. He Stopped Four Times on the Way
dek: Each stop was a puzzle, and the clock never paused while he solved it. Here is how long each one took.
body: Running a mile in about five minutes is fast for most people. George Scholey, a British speedcubing champion, decided to make it harder. Before every lap he had to solve a scrambled Rubik's Cube.

The attempt took place on October 12 on the track at Central Tech high school in Toronto, in a stiff wind. The format was simple and cruel. When the horn sounded he lifted a cover off a scrambled cube, solved it, then sprinted a 400-metre lap. Then another cube. Then another lap.
There was no pause button. Every second spent twisting the cube counted toward his mile time. To make the total an exact mile, the final lap was a little over nine metres longer than the others.

His cube solves took about 9, 10.5, 8.5 and 9.5 seconds, according to Guinness World Records. His laps came in at roughly 67 to 70 seconds each. His official time: 5 minutes 9.25 seconds for the fastest puzzle cube mile.

He trained for seven weeks, splitting the work between sprinting and cubing. Before the attempt he told Guinness he had solved a cube in 3.86 seconds and run a mile in 4:50 in a relay. Doing both at once is a different matter.

body.quote: Afterwards he told Guinness he was "absolutely buzzing."

body: It is not his first strange record. Scholey has solved 500 cubes on a skateboard, 6,931 cubes in 24 hours, and about 520 cubes while running the London Marathon. That last one has since been beaten by a Spanish runner who solved 561.
The cube mile is now his fourth multitasking speedcubing title, and the only one where he had to sprint.

headline: Police in South Carolina Chase Down Two Suspects on Foot. The Charge Sheet Is Something Else
dek: The pair were small, fast and loud. The department's write-up of the arrest is even better than the video.
body: Officers in Beaufort, South Carolina, found themselves in a foot pursuit against two suspects who refused to stop running. Both were very short and very fast.
They were piglets. Two of them, loose on the streets, darting away every time an officer got close.

A witness, Kate Morrison, filmed the chase, and the video was shared by the local tourism page Explore Beaufort. The Beaufort Police Department then posted its own version, with an official-looking summary to go with it.
The suspects were identified as the Bacon Bits. The offence was listed as fleeing and squealing. Police described the pair as career cri-ham-inals.
In the end both piglets were caught safely and handed back to their owner, which the department listed as the case's disposition.

body.quote: The department's verdict on the whole affair: "No ham was done."

headline: Earth Has Had a Second Moon Since April. Astronomers Only Just Confirmed It, and It's Already Packing to Leave
dek: It is smaller than a car, it loops around us on a wobbly path, and at first nobody was sure it was even a rock.
body: For most of this year Earth has quietly had company. A tiny space rock has been looping around the planet since about April, and almost nobody knew.

It was first spotted on August 20 by the Hungarian astronomer Krisztián Sárneczky. At the end of October the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center confirmed what the numbers suggested: the object had been temporarily captured by Earth's gravity. It now has the catchy official name 2026 QQ8.

When something that small shows up near Earth, the first question is whether it is natural at all. Old rocket stages and other bits of space hardware sometimes get mistaken for asteroids. This time the checks came back clean, and the Minor Planet Center said no link to any known artificial object had been found.

Size estimates vary from about one to two metres across, so it is somewhere between a fridge and a small car. Experts say it poses no danger. Anything that small would burn up in the atmosphere long before reaching the ground.

Do not expect to see it. Even at its closest it stays about one and a half times farther away than the Moon, tracing a loopy path around us while both of us travel around the Sun. Its own orbit around the Sun takes about 359 days, almost exactly an Earth year, which is how it ended up drifting alongside us in the first place.
The visit is short. Depending on whose model you trust, 2026 QQ8 slips free around mid-December or early in the new year and wanders off on its own again.

It does drop by roughly once a decade. It came close in 1965 without being caught, and astronomers expect another pass in 2058, again without a capture. So if you want to wave goodbye to Earth's second moon, this holiday season is your chance.

headline: Six Robots Take a 24-Hour Trial Shift at a Shanghai Shop. Not All of Them Get the Job
dek: More than two million people watched online. One robot's performance review would get a human let go on day one.
body: Chinese robot maker AGIBOT wanted to prove its humanoids are ready for real work, so it put six of its wheeled G2 robots in charge of a working convenience store in Shanghai's Xuhui district for a full day, from 10 a.m. on November 2 until 10 a.m. the next morning.

The company livestreamed the whole thing under the title 'Robots Never Clock Out', and more than two million people tuned in to watch them handle the lunch rush, the evening peak, the quiet overnight hours and the next day's breakfast crowd.

According to AGIBOT's own figures, the team got through 1,730 tasks. That included 683 customer-service chats, 147 coffees, 126 breakfasts, 369 product pickups, 277 shelf checks and 128 rounds of table cleaning.

At the end the robots were assessed like trainees, on time spent on duty, tasks completed, customer feedback and how they coped with surprises. Four passed and were promoted to 'official employees'. Two did not.

The first failure was a cleaning robot. A full rubbish bin was blocking its usual route, and instead of dealing with it, the robot wandered off its path, rolled out of the store and never came back to its post.

The second was in charge of watching the shelves and restocking them. Reports say it simply did not check often enough to keep up as products sold, and Chinese coverage described it as lacking initiative and showing too little enthusiasm on the job.

Both have been placed in an 'observation group' for more training, with the hope of being hired later. Analysts noted that much of the coverage was sponsored by AGIBOT and that no full task log was released, so the numbers come from the company itself. The walkout, however, was seen by everyone.

headline: The World's Loudest Woman Is Now Official. Her Career Began With a Bet About the Word 'Chips'
dek: She shouted one word, a measuring device caught it, and she still thinks she can go louder. The story of how she started is even better.
body: Town criers are the people in tricorn hats and red coats who ring a bell and shout announcements in English market towns. They are supposed to be loud. Brenda Willison, town crier of Newmarket in Suffolk, has now been certified as the loudest woman in the world.

On September 9 she shouted the traditional crier's call of "oyez", an old Anglo-Norman word meaning "hear ye", into a sound meter. It read 105.9 decibels. Guinness World Records compares that to standing next to a snowblower or a blaring car horn.

That earned her two titles: loudest town crier (female) and loudest shout by an individual (female). For comparison, the overall record belongs to Australian town crier Joseph McGrail-Bateup, who shouted "now" at 122.4 decibels in Canberra in May.
Willison has been crying since 1987, and she got the job in an unusual way. She was the catering manager at a country park near Peterborough that had two cafés about a mile and a half apart.

When a local advert went out looking for a town crier, her daughter entered her. The pitch, according to Guinness, was that her mum could stand outside one café, shout "chips", and be heard at the other one.
It worked. Nearly four decades later she has travelled the world, won crying competitions and performed duties for the Royal Family.

body.quote: She told Guinness she "wasn't at [her] best" on record day because she had a cold.

body: Even the judge was impressed. Adjudicator Emma Salt had a go at town crying herself and said it was the loudest she had ever been. She was still nowhere near Brenda.

headline: A Bagel Shop Left Its Back Door Open After Closing. Security Cameras Caught Who Walked Up to the Counter
dek: It came in through the parking lot, strolled through the kitchen and headed straight for the front of the store. The owner spotted it while installing an oven.
body: Bagel Dock Express in Southport, North Carolina, was closed for the day. Owner Jesse Driscoll was busy with a delivery crew installing a new oven, and the back door had been left open.
Security cameras show the next customer crossing the parking lot behind the building, coming in through that open door, making its way through the kitchen and walking up to the front counter.
It was an alligator, about three feet long, a youngster by alligator standards. Driscoll found it near the counter, panicked briefly, and called 911.

The men on site kept an eye on it and used a chair to help steer it, just in case. Southport Police and animal protection officers then arrived and escorted the reptile back outside. Nobody was hurt, including the alligator.

body.quote: "Never in a million years did I think I'd see an alligator," Driscoll told WWAY.

body: The shop took it well. In a Facebook post sharing the footage, it suggested word of its fresh bagels must have reached the swamp. Experts say young alligators sometimes wander into towns while moving between ponds and creeks, and this one most likely just took a wrong turn.

headline: It Started With Two Rubber Bands. Eleven Years Later, It Needed a Crane
dek: A Detroit man's hobby outgrew his garage, then a storage unit, and finally had to be weighed hanging from the sky.
body: Claude P. Moore of Detroit was diagnosed with hemophilia as a child, which meant a lot of time sitting in hospitals and doctors' waiting rooms. To pass the hours he started wrapping rubber bands into little balls.
In 2015 his coworkers made a suggestion: why not make a really big one? He took the challenge seriously. The new ball began, Guinness says, with just two small bands.

Year after year it grew. First it filled a spot in his garage. Then it outgrew the garage and had to move into its own storage container, where by the end it nearly touched the walls. Guinness describes it as about the size of a car.

In late August, after more than 11 years of work, dozens of volunteers rolled the ball out of its container. A crane lifted it and carried it to Belle Isle, the island park in the Detroit River, for the official weighing.

A Guinness adjudicator rode up in the crane cab to read the scale herself. The result was 11,578 pounds, or 5,251.69 kilograms. Guinness calls it elephant-sized, and the weight fits: it is about as heavy as a female African elephant.
The old record for the largest rubber band ball, 9,032 pounds, was set by Joel Waul of Florida back in 2008 and had stood for 18 years. Moore beat it by more than a ton.

body.quote: "If I say I'm going to do something, consider it done – my word is everything," Moore told Guinness World Records.

body: Nobody has said yet what happens to the ball now. Getting it back into storage will need the crane again.

headline: Someone Takes a Spade to an English Nature Reserve and Makes Off With Up to 5,000 Captives
dek: Researchers found a hollow where something precious used to be. Police are investigating, and a conservation charity compares it to stealing rare bird eggs.
body: In mid-October, researchers doing their regular checks at Chudleigh Knighton Heath, a nature reserve in south Devon, found a hollow in the ground where something should have been. The soil around it showed clear marks of a spade.
Someone had dug up and carried away an entire ant nest.

These were narrow-headed ants, the rarest ant species in England. The reserve, run by Devon Wildlife Trust, is their last stronghold in the country. The latest survey there counted 142 active nests, and now there is one fewer.

A single nest can hold between 1,000 and 5,000 ants, plus one or more breeding queens that can live for up to 25 years. Colonies grow slowly, so a mature nest represents years of work that can't simply be replaced.

body.quote: "This is a crime every bit as serious as illegal raids on wild bird eggs," said Julia Balfour of Devon Wildlife Trust.

body: The heath is a protected Site of Special Scientific Interest, and Devon and Cornwall Police say it is a criminal offence to deliberately or recklessly damage or disturb it. The theft has been reported to the force, and the trust is asking anyone who knows anything to come forward.

Nobody knows why anyone would want them. The species has been disappearing for a century as heathland was built on and farmed, and the trust and the charity Buglife had only this summer started a new project to protect it. Outside Devon, a few colonies survive in Scotland, including on the royal Balmoral estate.

headline: Man Tries On a $292,000 Watch and Sprints Off Still Wearing It. Three Days Later, a Parcel Arrives
dek: Inside was a very short handwritten message. Police still don't know who wrote it.
body: On the evening of Thursday, October 29, a man walked into Kamekichi, a luxury watch shop on the third floor of Nakano Broadway, a maze-like Tokyo shopping centre famous for its collectors' stores.
He spent about eight minutes looking around and asked to try on an Audemars Piguet valued at about 46 million yen, roughly $292,000. Then, with the watch still on his left wrist, he ran.

Staff chased him shouting thief as he leapt from escalator to escalator, all the way down from the third floor to the basement and out of the building. Security cameras caught him running down the street. Nobody was hurt.
On Sunday morning, November 1, a courier dropped a cardboard box at the shop. Inside was the watch, with no obvious damage. Employees checked the serial number. It was the one.
Tucked in with it was a handwritten note. According to Japanese television, it said simply: I'm sorry.
The parcel had been sent from Aichi Prefecture, hundreds of kilometres away, and carried a sender's name and address. Investigators believe both are fake.
Police are now trying to identify whoever posted the box, and whether it was the same man who fled the shop. As of early November, nobody had been arrested.

It is not the building's first watch theft this year. In August, four watches worth a combined 200 million yen were taken from a ground-floor shop in the same complex, and two men were arrested and charged.

hook: He ran off in a $292,000 watch. Then a parcel arrived.

headline: Swiss Scientists Teach a Robot Hand to Do Something No Hand Should Ever Do
dek: It weighs less than a bag of sugar, carries its own battery, and when it falls over, it gets straight back up.
body: Robot hands are usually attached to robot arms. The team at ETH Zurich's Soft Robotics Lab decided theirs did not need one.

Starting with an off-the-shelf robotic hand, the researchers strapped a battery, a tiny computer and a motion sensor onto its back. The whole thing weighs 818 grams, and nothing connects it to anything else.

Then they flipped it over and taught it to walk on its fingertips, scuttling across the floor just like Thing, the disembodied hand from The Addams Family. Almost every outlet that covered the research made the same comparison, and the videos are about as unsettling as you would expect.

body.h2: How do you teach a hand to walk?

body: The hand learned in a computer simulation first, through trial and error, and the skills were then moved onto the real hardware. It managed to crawl over 14 different surfaces, including wooden floors, metal grating, grass and gravel.

body.quote: Lead author Amirhossein Kazemipour explained the trickiest part: "The fingers have different lengths and a thumb off to one side, which makes walking awkward."

body: It can also right itself after toppling over, which it did in 21 out of 25 tries, and balance on some fingers while pressing keys with another. In one test it hit the correct arrow key 29 times out of 32, and it even played moves in the puzzle game Sokoban, with a human choosing the moves.

The team's plan is for a bigger robot to drop the hand near a tight space, let it crawl in to press a button or move something, and then come back. Detaching and reattaching on its own is still a future goal, and the study is a preprint that has not yet been peer-reviewed. So for now, at least, the hand does not wander off by itself.

img.alt: Two robotic hands with metal fingers and joints on display

hook: This robot hand doesn't need a body.

headline: A Zoo Animal Escaped Less Than a Day After Arriving. Seven Months Later, Staff Know Where She Is and Still Can't Bring Her Home
dek: Drones, a sniffer dog and 150 reported sightings later, she keeps turning up on camera. Even some of the cameras have gone missing.
body: In March, two young capybaras named Samba and Tango arrived at Marwell Zoo near Winchester, in southern England. Less than 24 hours later, on March 17, they had broken out of their temporary enclosure.
Tango was found nearby almost straight away. Samba, described by staff as the more adventurous sister, was not.

Capybaras are the world's largest rodents, native to South America and very much at home in water. Samba was soon spotted in the nearby village of Owslebury and later along the River Itchen, where people reported seeing her sunbathing on the bank and swimming downstream.

The zoo threw everything at it: daily ground searches, thermal drones over the villages, a sniffer dog and trail cameras. At one point two of those cameras were stolen, which made the job even harder.
In July the zoo brought in a male capybara, Ripple, to keep Tango company, while insisting he was no replacement for Samba. In August cameras caught her again, and more were installed.
In October came new pictures. They are blurry, but they prove Samba is still out there. The zoo won't say exactly where, because the photos were taken on private land.

The frustrating part is that staff now have a good idea where she is. They say they can't simply walk up and grab her, because frightening her could send her off somewhere new. Instead they have set up a feeding station to get her used to visiting one spot, and describe her return as a slow, carefully managed process.
Seven months in, England's most famous runaway rodent is still winning.

hook: She escaped on day one. Seven months later, still free.

headline: Drivers Kept Ignoring Crosswalks, So a Deputy Turned Herself Into a Giant Orange Traffic Cone
dek: Sixty-seven drivers failed the test anyway. One offered an excuse that was hard to sell.
body: In Stanislaus County, in California's Central Valley, the sheriff's office had a problem: too many drivers were not stopping for people on foot. A run of crashes, some of them fatal, had hit pedestrians in crosswalks across the county.
So its motorcycle unit tried something harder to ignore than a leaflet.

A deputy pulled on a huge orange traffic cone costume and stepped into marked crosswalks in Riverbank and Patterson, always leaving approaching drivers plenty of time to stop. Some did. Others rolled straight past the giant cone, and motorcycle deputies waiting nearby pulled them over.
Over two days, one in each city, deputies issued 67 citations for pedestrian violations and made two arrests for driving under the influence.

The sheriff's office posted video of the stops. In one, a deputy asks a driver whether he really did not notice his partner standing in the middle of the crosswalk dressed as a big orange cone. The driver says he saw her, but could not stop in time.

body.quote: "You had plenty of opportunity to stop and slow down, partner," the deputy replies.

body: The operation was paid for by a state traffic safety grant and timed for the darker evenings around Halloween and the end of daylight saving time, when pedestrians are hardest to see.
The sheriff's office urged drivers to stay alert, keep to the speed limit and yield to anyone in a crosswalk, costumed or not.

hook: This traffic cone is writing tickets.

headline: San Francisco Startup Pays $20 an Hour to Walk Its Dogs. Read the Small Print Before You Apply
dek: No experience needed, paid training and cash after every shift. You just have to be able to lift 33 pounds, for one very specific reason.
body: In early October a job ad appeared in a Bay Area jobs group on Facebook that looked like an easy gig: walk dogs around San Francisco for four to six hours at a time, $20 an hour, paid as soon as each shift ends. No experience necessary.

The catch was in the details. The dogs are robots, about $2,000 apiece from Chinese maker Unitree, and the employer is Dimensional, an AI startup in the city's Dogpatch neighbourhood that has bought more than 100 of them, plus around 50 humanoid robots.

The walkers steer the machines along outdoor routes with a remote or a phone app while the robots' cameras and sensors record everything. That data is used to teach robots how to find their way through real city streets.

Applicants had to be comfortable handling about 33 pounds of equipment. That is roughly what one of the robot dogs weighs, and there is a reason it matters: sometimes the dogs overheat or simply stop working in the middle of a walk, and then the walker has to carry the dog back to the office.

The company is building open-source software that would let AI agents control robots doing manual jobs like hauling boxes or working on building sites. Its 26-year-old founder, Stash Pomichter, told The New York Times that humans still doing that kind of heavy physical work is 'honestly barbaric'.

body.quote: But the walks taught him something humbling about the machines. "What we determined from our dog-walking experiment was that agents are still very bad at controlling hardware," Pomichter said.

body: In other words, the robots still need a person holding the leash, and now and then carrying the dog. The original Facebook post has since been deleted.

headline: Neighbour Hears a Car Horn Blaring at 12:30 a.m. and Looks Outside. Someone Is Sitting on It
dek: The driver couldn't get out, the owners couldn't unlock the doors, and the police had to improvise with a rope.
body: At about 12:30 one Monday morning in Juneau, Alaska, a car horn started blaring and would not stop. A neighbour looked out to see who was leaning on it.
It was a black bear, sitting on the horn inside Michael Wilson's Subaru. The neighbour called 911.

The bear had let itself in through an unlocked door. Then the door swung shut behind it, and it couldn't work out how to open it again. Wilson said it had already been into three cars on the street that night. His was the only one it got stuck in.

Officers woke the family to ask for the keys, but that didn't help. The bear had ripped out so much wiring that the doors would no longer unlock. So Juneau police tied a rope to the door and pulled it open from a safe distance.
Within five to ten minutes the bear was free. It ran off unhurt, leaving behind bent metal, shredded seats, torn door panels, and, according to Mistee Wilson, a little something extra on the floor.

body.quote: "So I got to hand it to Subaru. They made a good car," Michael Wilson told KTUU. "It couldn't get out."

body: The praise came with a sting: the family only had liability insurance, so the damage isn't covered. They say bears have been unusually bold this year after a winter of more than 200 inches of snow and a late spring cut into the berries and fish they normally eat.
Wilson's advice to his neighbours is simple: lock your car, and don't leave any food inside. Not even candy.

hook: The car horn wouldn't stop. Then they looked inside.

headline: Apple Finally Sells a Folding iPhone for $1,999. Within Days, Owners Start Posting Photos of the Fold
dek: Apple calls the early response 'incredibly positive'. The internet has already given the problem a nickname.
body: Samsung sold its first folding phone back in 2019. Apple took its time, and its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, went on sale only last week, with a 7.6-inch inner screen that opens like a book and a price tag of $1,999.

Within days, owners on Reddit and other forums began posting close-up photos of that inner screen. The pictures looked worryingly alike: a crack or a set of white lines running straight down the middle, right along the hinge.

Some said it happened within hours of unboxing. One owner said their screen simply gave out overnight. People started calling it 'crackgate', and the jokes wrote themselves, including one Reddit poster who said the phone had more crack than a plumber.

body.quote: Apple told reporters it is "aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units" and asked affected owners to contact AppleCare.

body: It added that most phones are not at risk, and that owners do not need to have paid for AppleCare+ to get a replacement. Apple has not said what is causing the problem.

Others have been guessing. A teardown by repair site iFixit pointed to parts that may press too hard on the screen, independent tests found dust can sneak into the hinge despite the phone's dust rating, and one YouTube analysis suggested the hinge has a weak spot.

There is one more twist. 9to5Mac, which tracked the complaints, noticed that some of the cracked-screen posts flooding Reddit appear to be fake, AI-generated images. Several are real, though, which leaves Apple's newest phone with a problem in exactly the place it was supposed to shine.

headline: Dozens March on an Insurance Giant's Boston Headquarters. Their Enemy Is Small, Yellow and Fluffy
dek: The organiser called it the next Boston Tea Party. Then a lone counter-protester turned up in costume.
body: On a Sunday afternoon in late October, several dozen people gathered outside Liberty Mutual's headquarters in Boston carrying protest signs. Some read 'Liberty from Biberty'. Others showed a cartoon face crossed out.
Their target was Liberty Biberty, the round, fuzzy yellow mascot the insurance company has been putting in its TV adverts. A lot of viewers find him unbearable, and the ads painfully repetitive.

The protest was organised by Connor Harvey, a 19-year-old YouTuber from Wilmot, New Hampshire. His video 'Death of Mascots' tore into the character's looks, and his call to march on headquarters pulled in more than 600,000 views.

Protesters told reporters the campaign felt lazy, and compared Biberty unfavourably with rival mascots like the Geico Gecko and Jake from State Farm. Harvey livestreamed the event and promised to keep it peaceful.

body.quote: "This is a revolution, this is the next Boston Tea Party," Harvey declared, although he admitted the whole thing started as a joke and was unlikely to change the company's mind.

body: The mascot did have one supporter. A lone counter-protester, Calvin Holmes, showed up dressed as Liberty Biberty himself and was jeered by the crowd. He argued that everyone there was discriminating against 'this puffball' just for the way he was born.

Liberty Mutual did not comment on the protest. It has, however, said that early testing showed Liberty Biberty scoring above average for grabbing attention and making people remember the brand. A crowd, a viral video and a costumed defender on the steps of its headquarters suggest the testing may have been right.

hook: Their enemy is small, yellow and fluffy.

headline: At 3 a.m. a Caller Tells Police: 'They're Robbing the Trains.' The Loot Turns Out to Be Tiny
dek: Officers stopped a pickup loaded with 350 boxes. The cargo inside was worth about $54,000, and it all fits in your hand.
body: In the small hours of October 20, a resident of Colton, an old railway town east of Los Angeles, rang the police with a tip that sounded like it came straight out of a Western.

body.quote: "Yeah, they're robbing the trains down here at the end of Maple Street," the caller told dispatchers, according to the Los Angeles Times.

body: A BNSF freight train was sitting near Mason Street, and the caller said people were loading boxes from it into a black pickup truck.
One officer happened to be parked under a nearby bridge. He spotted a black Chevrolet Silverado, followed it and pulled it over.
The truck was crammed with Hot Wheels. Officers counted 350 boxes of the little die-cast cars, each holding several models, with an estimated total value of around $54,000.

The driver, a 20-year-old man, was booked on suspicion of burglary, possession of stolen property and grand theft, and was later released on bail. Detectives are still trying to work out whether he had help.
The Colton Police Department could not resist the obvious joke. Its Facebook post about the arrest announced that his wheels just weren't hot enough to get away.

A department spokesperson told reporters an arrest of that size was a big deal for the city. Freight-train break-ins are a long-running headache along Southern California's rail lines, but few of them come with a pun this good.

headline: Food Delivery App Lets AI Draw Pictures of the Menu. Customers Order a Jacket Potato and Get Something Very Different
dek: It began with a breakfast sandwich from a café in Northern Ireland. By the time anyone noticed, a bowl of tiger prawns had grown fur.
body: Plenty of small takeaways never get round to photographing their dishes, so Just Eat, one of the UK's biggest food delivery apps, came up with a shortcut. Where a restaurant had no picture, an AI tool would read the name of the dish and generate one, with a small 'AI-generated' label in the corner.
The idea was to save independent restaurants the cost of a photographer. The problem is that a name on a menu is not always a description, and the AI took every word literally.

A café in Northern Ireland sells a classic local breakfast: bacon and egg on soda bread. The app's version showed a tall glass of fizzy cola with a fried egg, rashers of bacon and a sausage bobbing around in it.

Once screenshots hit Reddit and Instagram, users went hunting for more, and there were plenty. A jacket potato became a winter puffer jacket printed with potatoes. A 'chip muffin', a takeaway's name for a chip butty, turned into sweet muffins with fries baked inside.

Garlic bread plain, misspelt on one menu as 'plane', came out as an aeroplane made of toasted garlic bread. A cheese roll turned into sushi with slabs of cheddar. A pot of burger sauce had a tiny burger sitting in it, and a dish of tiger prawns arrived as a bowl of actual tiger cubs swimming in sauce.

body.quote: Just Eat apologised and paused the trial. A spokesperson told The Journal: "We're sorry for any inaccurate images that have been posted."

body: The company is now pulling the strange pictures from its listings and says restaurants can always upload their own photos. It has not given up on AI images, though. It says it will keep working on the tool, so somewhere out there the tiger cubs may yet return.

headline: Florida Campus Police Get a $148,000 One-Seat Flying Machine. Then Someone Looks Up Their Crime Stats
dek: It is named after a cartoon dog, flies for about 20 minutes and is still waiting for permission to go on patrol.
body: The police department at Florida Polytechnic University in Lakeland has unveiled what it says is the first piloted electric aircraft ever added to a US law enforcement fleet.

The machine is a Jetson ONE, a small Swedish-built electric craft that takes off straight up like a drone but carries one person sitting in an open frame. The university's version is painted black and white, with police decals and a light bar, and has been renamed Astro, after the dog in The Jetsons.
It weighs 154 pounds without its pilot or battery, tops out at about 63 mph and can stay in the air for roughly 20 minutes on a charge. Reports put the price at around $148,000.

body.h2: So what will it be chasing?

body: The university says Astro could be used for keeping an eye on campus, reaching spots that are hard to get to and helping out after storms, for example by dropping off supplies. It will also double as a teaching tool for aerospace engineering students.

body.quote: Police Chief Aaron Murray said: "Advanced air mobility is a technology on the rise, and we can either choose to be proactive or reactive as it develops."

body: Critics online were less sure. Futurism dug into the campus police's own annual crime report and found that the most common offence on campus in 2025 was the 'liquor law referral', with 13 cases. The department also already runs at least five surveillance drones.

For now, the question is mostly academic. Astro is still waiting for final approval from the Federal Aviation Administration before it can be used in actual police work. Futurism pointed out that it has a famous ancestor: the US Army's 1950s flying platforms, which were also meant to lift a single soldier into the air, and were quietly dropped.

headline: Police Are Called to a Sidewalk Standoff in Philadelphia. One Side Is a 78-Year-Old Professor. The Other Is Carrying Someone's Lunch
dek: She calls it a protest. Police call it disorderly conduct. The other party has declined to comment.
body: Just after 1 p.m. on October 14, Philadelphia police were called to the 1200 block of Filbert Street, near Reading Terminal Market, after a report of 'criminal mischief'.

When officers arrived, they found Carolyn Marvin, a 78-year-old retired communications professor from the University of Pennsylvania, standing on the sidewalk and refusing to step aside. What she was refusing to make way for was an autonomous food delivery robot working for Uber Eats.

Officers told her several times to move. She would not, saying she had a First Amendment right to protest on a public sidewalk. She was handed a criminal violation notice for disorderly conduct as a small crowd looked on.
This was not a chance encounter. Marvin had blocked the robots before, as a protest against the growing fleet of machines rolling around Center City since Uber Eats brought them in earlier this year.
She told reporters she objects on three counts: the robots take work from low-paid human delivery drivers, they crowd the sidewalks, and their cameras are constantly filming the public.

body.quote: "I was under the impression that I had more rights than the robot did," Marvin said. "I wasn't impeding any persons. I was impeding a machine."

body: She plans to fight the charge in court. Asked by a local TV station whether she will keep standing in front of robots, her answer was short: 'Why not?'

headline: His Campaign Signs Said 'I Barely Want to Do This.' Then the Votes Came In
dek: His website admitted he had no idea what he was doing. A councillor with 15 years at city hall was about to find out how much voters cared.
body: Most people running for office try to sound eager. Brady Rogers, a 33-year-old small business owner in Kelowna, British Columbia, went the other way.

His lawn signs read "I barely want to do this", "Just trying to pay my rent", "Fine. I'll do it" and "How hard can it be". His campaign website asked itself whether he enjoyed politics (no), whether he knew what he was doing (no) and whether he was qualified (also no).
The signs went viral far beyond the Okanagan. Kelowna's municipal election on October 17 had 37 candidates chasing eight council seats, so standing out was half the battle.
When the preliminary results came in, Rogers had 12,635 votes. That put him fourth out of 37, comfortably inside the winning eight.

The person who missed out was Maxine DeHart, a councillor first elected in 2011 who was going for a fifth term. She finished ninth with 11,165 votes, just 305 short of the last seat. Five newcomers and three incumbents made it onto the new council, on a turnout of about 31 percent.
So was the whole thing a joke? Only partly. Rogers explained that the self-mockery was deliberate and that he does have useful experience in business and problem-solving.

body.quote: "I'm being a little bit tongue-in-cheek when I say I'm unqualified," Rogers told Global News.

body: He says his priorities are homelessness, housing costs and support for small businesses, and after the results came in he promised to take the job seriously. The man who barely wanted to do it now has a four-year term to prove how hard it can be.

headline: Two Knights in Full Armour Charge at Each Other in a London Park. Their Horses Are Rental E-Bikes
dek: Hundreds turned up, millions watched online, and the bike company had to issue a statement. Then a real professional jouster gave his verdict.
body: On a Saturday in mid-October, hundreds of people gathered in London Fields, a park in Hackney, east London, for a free event that sounded like a joke. Two men in full suits of armour would fight a medieval joust, lances and all.

The catch was the horses. There weren't any. Artist and online personality Jack Carden and his opponent, who performs as Camtholomew the First, rode the green Lime electric bikes that Londoners rent by the minute to get to work.
Clips of the two knights wobbling toward each other with lances under their arms spread fast online and were viewed millions of times. Carden called the whole thing performance art.

Lime, which owns the bikes, was asked what it thought of its fleet being used as warhorses. Its answer, given to the BBC, was polite but clear: the bikes are for getting around the city, not for medieval combat.

body.quote: "While we appreciate the medieval spirit, safety must always come first," a Lime spokesperson told the BBC.

body: That did not stop the sequel. The organisers announced Lime Bike Jousting 2, subtitled No Horses, No Mercy, and LBC reported that more than 5,000 people RSVPed within a day. Police signed off on the gathering about 90 minutes before it started on Halloween, and only then was the location revealed: London Fields again.

Then the experts weighed in. ITV asked Andy Deane, captain of the jousting team at the Royal Armouries in Leeds, who does this for a living on real horses. He had no complaints. He called the e-bike version absolutely a legitimate form of jousting.
So London now has an unofficial new sport. The armour is real, the lances are real, and the steeds have a pay-per-minute app.

headline: Burglar Breaks In and Steals Just One Thing: A Kid's VR Headset. Then He Puts It On
dek: The family had barely unpacked. A few hours later they were watching the thief from their own phone.
body: A family in Ocoee, a suburb west of Orlando, had only just moved into their new house when someone crept in overnight through the sliding glass door at the back. There were boxes everywhere, but the intruder ignored nearly all of them.
He left with a single item: the children's virtual reality headset.

What he could not have known was that the headset was still paired with one of the parents' phones. The family liked to watch their kids' games through a live stream on their mobile, and that link was still active.

So the moment the burglar switched on his new toy, the family, and soon the police, had a front-row view of whatever he was looking at. The picture showed the inside of a parked car and, beyond it, a house with a very distinctive green roof.
The headset has no GPS, so the roof was the only real clue. Luckily, Ocoee Police Sergeant Kevin Birdsong had grown up in the area and recognised it.
Within about an hour, officers were knocking on the door of that house. The man inside handed the headset over.

Police identified him as 18-year-old Ja'Mir Edmond Baker. He was taken to the Orange County jail on an existing warrant, which reports say concerned an iPad allegedly taken from a parked car months earlier. The headset went back to the kids.
Experts quoted after the case had simple advice for everyone else: leave tracking and remote monitoring switched on, and lock the sliding door.

headline: A Dutch Woman Wins the World Porridge Championship in Scotland. Her Secret Came in Her Suitcase
dek: The traditional category allows only three ingredients: oats, water and salt. She beat 30 rivals from 14 countries by thinking hard about one of them.
body: Every October the Highland village of Carrbridge hosts the World Porridge Making Championship. The winner takes home the Golden Spurtle, named after the wooden stick Scots use to stir their oats.

The main contest is strict. In the traditional category you may use oats, water and salt, and nothing else. No milk, no sugar, no honey. With only three ingredients allowed, small details decide everything.

This year the title went to Gina Saarberg, 28, from Zutphen in the Netherlands. She beat 30 competitors from 14 countries, including Norway and Australia, in front of a judging panel led by former Gleneagles chef Neil Mugg.
Her oats were Dutch pinhead oats from a company called De Halm. Her salt was ordinary salt. But her water did not come from a Scottish tap. She brought it with her from home.

body.quote: "It's very soft and I think the mineral content may have something to do with it," she told BBC Scotland, as reported by DutchNews.

body: Saarberg started making porridge as a student to save money on food. Over time she switched from rolled oats to oatmeal, which she says made it creamier, almost like rice pudding. She only started adding salt for competitions, and says it brings out more flavour.
She qualified by winning the Dutch national championship earlier in the year, using the same recipe, the same oats and, yes, the same water.
The speciality prize, where anything goes, went to Australian Rob Reid for a Sicilian-Scottish porridge cannoli. Scotland's national dish keeps travelling a long way to be beaten in its own village.

headline: Police Pull Over Two Men on a Busy City Street. Their Ride Was Not Exactly a Vehicle
dek: It seated two, had no doors, and took both passengers to steer.
body: Officers in the Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police Department's Entertainment District Unit see plenty of strange things on a weekend night around the city's bars and clubs. On Friday, September 25, they saw something new rolling down South Tryon Street.
Two men were cruising along the road on a couch.
Not a couch strapped to a truck, either. The pair had balanced a small love seat across two rented Lime electric scooters, and it took both of them working together to keep it pointed the right way.
Officers stopped them, and on October 1 the department shared the moment on Facebook, assuring readers that yes, it really was an actual couch.

body.quote: Police wrote that they had stopped "two gentlemen traveling down S. Tryon Street on a couch."

body: The post praised the creativity but pointed out the problem: a sofa gliding through traffic could easily distract the drivers of real cars. It suggested leaving mobile furniture displays to IKEA.

The internet did the rest. The post collected around 1,700 comments and reactions in its first three hours, with one commenter calling it truly couch surfing and another asking whether sofas need insurance.
Police did not name the men or say whether either got a ticket. They did say it was a first for the department.

headline: French Mayor Signs an Official Order: Nobody in Town Is Allowed to Get Sick
dek: Residents who feel something coming on are told to postpone it. The mayor, a former family doctor, admits the whole thing is absurd. That is the point.
body: Marmande is a market town of tomatoes and vineyards in south-western France. As of this autumn, it is also a place where, on paper, falling ill is against the rules.
Mayor Joël Hocquelet, a Socialist who used to work as a GP, has published a formal municipal decree declaring that it is forbidden for anyone to be ill within the town's boundaries.
The decree even comes with advice. Anyone who feels an illness coming on is asked to put it off until they can get an appointment at the local hospital.

body.h2: Why a doctor would ban being sick

body: The order has no legal force, and Hocquelet happily calls it absurd. It is a protest, and the target is what is happening to the town's hospital.

The Marmande-Tonneins hospital, which serves about 110,000 people including part of the neighbouring Gironde, was placed under temporary administration by the regional health authority in January because of serious money problems. From early 2027, departments such as cardiology, digestive medicine and diabetes care may be moved to the hospital in Agen, a long drive away.

Hocquelet, who chairs the hospital's supervisory board in turns with the mayor of nearby Tonneins, warns that further cuts could cost the town its full emergency department and its laboratory, leaving the hospital a shell of itself. Newcomers to the area already struggle to find a family doctor.

He says people are welcome to laugh at the decree as long as they also notice the problem behind it. Large parts of rural France are now described as medical deserts, and he wants the ban to sound the alarm in Paris.

He is not the first to try it. In January 2025 the mayor of Belcastro, a small town in southern Italy, issued a very similar ban on illness to protest about a health centre that was often closed. The joke, it seems, travels well.

headline: Thieves Break Into a French Farm, Knock Out the Camera and Take €25,000 of Goods. They Were Very Picky
dek: They passed over the younger stock. The farmer is convinced they knew exactly what they were looking for.
body: At Bergerie du Tilh, a sheep farm in Artigueloutan near Pau in south-west France, the most valuable room on the property is not the farmhouse. It is the cool ageing room where the cheese sits for months until it is ready.
Two people forced their way into that room, put a security camera out of action and left with about 250 wheels of sheep's-milk tomme.

They did not just grab whatever was closest to the door. According to French broadcaster TF1, the thieves went for the older, darker wheels, the ones that had matured longest and sell for the most. Each wheel goes for between €80 and €130 depending on its age.
Producer Régis Junqua put the loss at roughly €25,000. He told TF1 the intruders seemed calm and well prepared, and described them as professionals.

Getting rid of 250 marked cheeses is harder than it sounds, because every wheel carries the producer's stamp. Alexandre Salles, co-president of a French cheesemakers' federation, suggested a buyer could simply strip off the rind, cut the cheese into pieces and sell it where nobody would recognise it.
It is not an isolated taste for dairy. In late 2025, Italian police investigated the disappearance of around 200 wheels of Parmigiano Reggiano from a cooperative near Bologna.

A France 24 press review in November relayed a report in The Times that cheese has become France's most stolen food, with thieves said to like it partly because the penalties are far lighter than for dealing drugs. No arrests had been reported in the Pyrenees case.

headline: Two Men Took the Maker of Reese's to Court Over Their Halloween Candy. A Judge Has Now Said No Twice
dek: Nobody said it tasted bad. The complaint was about something the chocolate didn't have.
body: Every autumn, Reese's Peanut Butter Pumpkins arrive in shops wrapped in orange packaging printed with a cheerful carved jack-o'-lantern: triangle eyes, a nose and a toothy grin.
Unwrap one, though, and the chocolate inside is a smooth, plain, entirely faceless lump.

Two Florida men, Nathan Vidal and Eduardo Granados, decided that amounted to false advertising. In 2024 they filed a proposed class action against Hershey, saying they had bought the candy for its novelty carvings and paid extra for a face that never turned up.
In September 2025, U.S. District Judge Melissa Damian threw out the first version of the complaint but let them try again. They did. In September 2026 she dismissed it a second time.

body.quote: The judge found the men had received edible Reese's products "of the type and quantity advertised," and that what they described was "subjective disappointment" rather than a real financial loss.

body: Their claim that they had paid a premium ran into trouble too. They bought the candy at Publix but used prices from Walmart, Target and Hershey's own online store to make their case. And the carved face on the wrapper is labelled, in small print, a decorating suggestion.
The pumpkins are not the only alleged offenders. Hershey has faced similar complaints about Reese's ghosts with no faces and Reese's footballs with no laces.
The men's lawyer told Reuters they plan to appeal, saying Florida consumers deserve to get what they pay for. Hershey said it does not comment on litigation.

headline: A Private Jet Lands at a Quiet Countryside Airfield. It Is Not the Airfield It Was Looking For
dek: The airport the pilots wanted was 11 miles away. The one they picked was home to American bombers, and security was waiting.
body: On the morning of Saturday, September 12, a small business jet took off from London City Airport for a short hop west into the Cotswolds. The aircraft, a German-registered Cessna Citation run by the private jet company VistaJet, was due to land at Cotswold Airport at Kemble, a former RAF field now used by private flyers.
Just over half an hour later it touched down safely on a long runway in the Gloucestershire countryside. The trouble was that it was the wrong runway.

body.h2: Wrong base, wrong country's air force

body: The jet had landed at RAF Fairford, about 11 miles east of Kemble. Fairford may carry the Royal Air Force name, but it is run by the United States Air Force and currently hosts a detachment of B-1B Lancer strategic bombers.

An unannounced civilian plane rolling down a bomber runway is not something base security takes lightly. As soon as it touched down, an emergency response kicked in, and plane spotters outside the fence posted pictures of security vehicles gathering around the little jet.

According to the aviation site The Aviationist, the pilot realised the mistake quickly and wanted to leave straight away. Security had other ideas. Nobody was going anywhere until the interviews were done and the paperwork was filled in.
Roughly three hours later the jet was finally allowed to take off again, at about 12:10 p.m. Its flight to the airport it had meant to visit in the first place took about four minutes.

Nobody suggested the landing was anything other than an honest mistake. RAF Fairford did not immediately comment. Similar slip-ups are rare but not unknown: a civilian Pilatus turboprop landed at an RAF base in Wales by mistake in 2020.

headline: Student Misses a $1 Million Kick on Live TV. Then a Hollywood Star Steps In
dek: He camped out all night for one shot at a fortune, kicked barefoot, and missed. Then a famous voice in the crowd changed the rules.
body: ESPN's College GameDay show has a segment called Kicking Is Easy. A fan picked from the crowd gets one field goal attempt, and if it goes through, host Pat McAfee pays out a huge prize. It is usually a sad moment for someone.

Before Texas played Ohio State on September 12, the show was in Austin. Connor Kacena-Merrell, a Texas freshman who grew up near Indianapolis, camped out the night before so he would be among the first 300 fans eligible for the draw. His name came up.

The prize was $1 million. Before he kicked, he announced that he would give half of anything he won to Building Tomorrow, an Indianapolis charity that funds schooling in East Africa. Then he took off his shoes and kicked barefoot.

The ball missed. Normally that is the end of it. But the actor Matthew McConaughey, a famous Longhorns fan, was on the set, and he talked McAfee into giving the student another go. McConaughey added $100,000 to the pot himself. Analyst Kirk Herbstreit matched it.
So the second attempt was worth $1.2 million, the biggest prize in the show's history. Kacena-Merrell put it through.

body.quote: "The best time to plant a tree was yesterday. The second best time is right now," he said, explaining the donation, according to Nexstar.

body: The day was not over. The charity arm of Tito's Vodka offered another $1 million to good causes if he could make a 35-yard kick during a break in the first quarter of the game. He made that one on his first try. Half went to the Central Texas Food Bank and half to Building Tomorrow.

Add it all up and the morning he almost went home with nothing raised around $2.2 million, most of it for charity. He says his own share will go mostly on out-of-state tuition, with a summer trip with friends on top.
