headline: Steel Conker Scandal: 82-Year-Old King Conker Accused of Cheating With a Metal Chestnut
dek: His opponent's conker shattered in one hit. Then a steel one turned up in the champion's pocket.
body: Every sport has its doping scandal. The World Conker Championships have a steel chestnut.

More than 200 people entered the 2024 championships, held on October 13 at a pub in the English village of Southwick. The rules are simple: thread a horse chestnut onto a string, take turns whacking your opponent's conker, and try to smash it.

The men's title went to an 82-year-old veteran known to everyone as King Conker. His opponent in the final was less than thrilled, and raised the alarm after his own conker exploded in a single strike.
Organisers confirmed that a steel conker had been found in the champion's pocket. He denied any wrongdoing.

The committee investigated, reviewing photos, video and statements from judges and umpires. On October 21 they cleared him, accepting that he carried the metal conker purely to amuse people as part of his King Conker persona.

body.quote: The committee's chair said four judges had watched him so closely that cheating was absolutely impossible.

body: The beaten finalist accepted the verdict gracefully. And in the end, King Conker did not take the overall crown anyway. That went to a 34-year-old woman from Indianapolis, who beat him to become the first American champion since the contest began in 1965.

headline: Museum's Beer-Can Artwork Thrown in the Bin by a Worker Who Thought It Was Litter
dek: The cans were hand-painted masterpieces. The new lift engineer saw two empty beers and did the tidy thing.
body: Modern art is often accused of looking like rubbish. At one Dutch museum, someone took that literally.

The LAM museum in Lisse was displaying a work by French artist Alexandre Lavet called All The Good Times We Spent Together. It appears to be two empty, dented beer cans. In fact, they are meticulously hand-painted with acrylics, a piece the museum says took enormous time and effort.
To surprise visitors, the museum placed the cans in its glass lift shaft, as though someone had carelessly left them behind. The illusion worked a little too well.
A lift engineer who had just started working at the museum spotted the cans, decided they were trash, and threw them away.
A curator returning from a short break noticed the artwork was gone and found it in a bin bag full of swept-up litter, just before it was taken away for good. Both cans survived intact.

body.quote: A museum spokesperson said there were no hard feelings, and that the engineer was only doing his job.

body: The cans were cleaned up and moved to a traditional plinth so the artwork could rest after its adventure. The museum's director said the whole point of the collection is to make people look at everyday objects in a new way. Mission, arguably, accomplished.

headline: Orcas Bring Back 1987's Hottest Fashion Trend: Wearing Dead Salmon as Hats
dek: A killer whale was photographed with a fish balanced on its head, reviving a mystery that has baffled scientists for nearly 40 years.
body: Fashion is cyclical, and apparently that applies to killer whales too.

On October 25, 2024, a photographer near Point No Point in Puget Sound captured a male orca swimming along with a dead salmon perched neatly on top of his head. The nonprofit Orca Network reported the sighting, and researchers identified the whale as J27, nicknamed Blackberry, a 32-year-old male from J pod.
J pod belongs to the endangered southern resident killer whales, a population of about 71 animals split into three pods that eat nothing but fish. And they have a history with this particular look.

body.h2: The summer of the salmon hat

body: In 1987, a female in K pod started wearing salmon on her head. Within months, the trend had spread to the other two pods. Then, almost as suddenly as it began, it vanished, and it was barely seen again for decades.

The new sighting came during an unusually big chum salmon run, the same week J pod spent a rare ten days in a row being spotted in the area. That may matter, because nobody actually knows why orcas do this. Theories include playing with spare food, saving a snack for later, or some kind of social food-sharing.

body.quote: One biologist summed up the science honestly: it is all speculation.

body: She has seen southern residents wear the look four or five times since 2005, and says it at least suggests a whale with plenty to eat. Other experts are not ready to call a full comeback. One photo, they note, does not make a trend. Fashion critics in the Pacific Northwest remain divided.

headline: Man Lives 120 Days in a Steel Capsule at the Bottom of the Sea, Then Pops Up for Champagne and a Cigar
dek: No shower, four cameras and a copy of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea by the bed.
location: Off the Caribbean coast of Panama
body: Most people find a week of working from home isolating. One man spent four months working from the bottom of the ocean.
On January 24, 2025, a 59-year-old German aerospace engineer climbed out of a capsule submerged 11 metres below the surface off Panama's Caribbean coast. He had been living inside it for 120 days.

His underwater home measured about 30 square metres and was connected by a tube with a narrow spiral staircase to a chamber above the waves, where food, visitors and a doctor could reach him. Inside he had a bed, a toilet, a TV, a computer, internet and an exercise bike. What he did not have was a shower.
Four cameras recorded his every move, both to keep an eye on his mental health and to prove he never sneaked up to the surface. Witnesses monitored him day and night.

A Guinness adjudicator confirmed the record for the longest time living underwater without decompression, beating the previous mark of 100 days. He kept a copy of Jules Verne's Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea by his bed and says he admires Captain Nemo.

body.quote: He said the point was to show that the ocean could one day be a place for humans to live.

body: He celebrated his return to dry land with champagne, a cigar and a jump straight back into the Caribbean. He admitted he was a little sad the adventure was over. Whoever got to sit next to him afterwards, given the shower situation, was not asked for comment.

headline: Man Facing Car-Theft Charges Drives a Stolen Car to His Own Car-Theft Hearing
dek: An auto theft task force watched him park. He never made it in front of the judge.
body: There are bad ideas, and then there is driving a stolen car to court for your stolen-car case.

A 41-year-old man from Soledad, California, was due to appear at the Monterey County courthouse in Salinas on a pending auto theft charge. At around 11 a.m. on Tuesday, March 24, 2026, he pulled into the courthouse parking area, on time and ready to face the music.
The car he arrived in had been reported stolen in San Jose.

As luck would have it for everyone except him, members of a regional auto theft task force, known as MADCAT, were watching as he parked. Of all the parking lots in California, he had picked the one where car-theft specialists were literally on duty.

body.quote: Deputies met him right outside the courtroom where his car-theft case was about to be heard.

body: He was arrested before he could set foot in front of the judge. The sheriff's office said the arrest went smoothly.

He was booked into Monterey County Jail on suspicion of unlawfully taking a vehicle, committing a felony while out on bail, and driving on a suspended licence. His original case is presumably now the least of his problems.

headline: It's Official: A Judge Has Ruled That Tacos and Burritos Are Sandwiches
dek: A strip-mall rule said sandwiches only. A taco shop owner fought it for two years, and won.
body: The internet has argued for years about whether a hot dog is a sandwich. In Indiana, a court has settled a far bolder question.

The owner of a local restaurant called The Famous Taco wanted to open a second location in a Fort Wayne strip mall. There was one problem. The plaza was bound by an agreement with a neighbouring condo association that allowed only a sandwich-bar-style restaurant selling made-to-order, subway-style sandwiches. No alcohol. No outdoor seating. And, everyone assumed, no tacos.
The rule was reportedly designed to keep national fast-food chains out. When the local plan commission refused to amend it to explicitly allow tacos and burritos, the owner sued.

body.h2: The ruling heard round the lunch hour

body: After more than two years of legal back and forth, Allen Superior Court Judge Craig Bobay delivered his verdict in May 2024.

body.quote: Tacos and burritos, the judge wrote, are Mexican-style sandwiches.

body: Because the agreement never said the sandwiches had to be American-style, the judge concluded the taco shop had been allowed all along, and the whole fight to amend it had been unnecessary.
The owner said he was relieved and expected the new location to open within a few months. The hot dog question, sadly, remains open.

headline: Fugitive Otter 841 Keeps Stealing Surfboards and Outsmarting Wildlife Officials
dek: Nets, traps and a decoy surfboard all failed. Santa Cruz's most wanted sea otter just dived off and kept going.
body: Surfers off Santa Cruz spent the summer of 2023 dealing with an unusual hazard. Not sharks, not rip currents, but a five-year-old sea otter with a surfboard habit.

Known officially as Otter 841, the female southern sea otter developed a routine: swim up to a surfer, climb aboard, refuse to leave, and start biting the board. In one case she chewed off part of a board's nose.
Crime may run in the family. Otter 841 was born in captivity and released into the wild in June 2020, and her mother had also been captured for harassing kayakers.

Teams from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Monterey Bay Aquarium spent weeks trying to catch her. They towed a baited surfboard toward their boat. They tried several kinds of nets. They deployed an underwater trap operated by divers.
Every time they got close, she simply dived off and swam away. Officials could not net her in open water, and sedating her was off the table because she could drown.

body.quote: A local photographer said the failed capture attempts had become almost comical.

body: Federal wildlife officials called her behaviour highly unusual and suggested hormones or people feeding her might be to blame. Meanwhile, she gained a fan club that gathered on the cliffs every day to watch. No humans were hurt, and as of late July she was still at large. Southern sea otters, once down to about 50 animals in 1938, now number around 3,000. At least one of them is very good at surfing.
